doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Self-taught players with great ears
summary: Rowe and Pallo trade stories of players who found good chords without knowing their names, such as the San Francisco example.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Makes me think of a guitar player I played with once who was very self-taught and if he played a chord that was really great and I want to know what it is, and I’d say what is that and he’d show me his hand. You know?
But he didn’t know what it was.
He didn’t know what the notes were, he didn’t know what it was, and I don’t even think he could have told me the notes unless I had him play one at a time. But he was great. He had great ears.

Oh well see that’s what we were just talking about, great ears. It’s like this gentleman came up and played San Francisco [sings] I left my heart in San Francisco. He’d say — we’ll put it in C just make it easy — he would just go from C to G seven, instead of using the seven. It sounded pretty good though. And then of course he never played any of the flat fives or thirteenth or whatever. But at times it sounded so good that he said well it’s not right but it’s good. And I don’t know how but it came out.
It sounded hillbillyish or — I don’t mean to put that down — but it sounded more country. More country.
